turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Niamh. Take a seat. What's been troubling you?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the stomach, doctor, and the sleep is gone to pot. I'm worried sick about it, if I'm honest.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. Start with the stomach. Where do you feel it, and what is it like?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): A burning pain, just under the breastbone. It comes and goes, but it's worse when I lie down at night.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has that been going on?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah sure, since Diwali, or after that. I can't pin it down. Last winter, or the one before, maybe. My neighbour had a do, there was spice, but the date is gone out of my head entirely.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's grand, we won't force a date. Does anything settle it?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Gaviscon helps a small bit, the pink bottle from the chemist. Not for long, mind you.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the sleep?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Desperate. I'm awake half the night with the burning, and then the mind is racing. The bus was late this morning and I was in a heap, but that's not it. Is this something bad, will you tell me straight?

[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm thinking this sounds acid-related, heartburn or a bit of gastritis, but I want the red-flag things ruled out before I say that too firmly. Any vomiting of blood, or black stools?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing like that. God, no.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight dropping off without trying?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the weight is the same. I'm still in the same trousers.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any nausea with it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Sometimes, not really. I don't know how to answer that one.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll leave that one. Any fever, or pain going through to the back?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever. And it doesn't go through to the back. It's just the front.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Let me have a feel of the tummy, if that's alright. Lie back a little.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Soft. Tender just under the breastbone when I press. No guarding, nothing that feels acute.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Is tender a bad sign? Does that mean an ulcer?
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tenderness there fits with irritation from acid. An ulcer is still on the list, I won't pretend it isn't, but there's nothing today that says we rush you in.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): What about the tablets I'm already on? I take a water tablet in the morning for the blood pressure. Most days, though I do forget it sometimes, I'll admit.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's useful. Do you know the name of the water tablet, or the dose?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't. It's just the water tablet, the box is at home in the press. And for the head I take Crocin, two tablets, maybe, when it's at me. Not every day.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Crocin is paracetamol, that's fine. Anything else for the stomach in the past?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): The purple capsules. I was given them ages ago and I stopped them. They gave me a headache, so I left them off.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you remember the name on those purple ones?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't. Purple capsules, that's all I have. And I use the Gaviscon now and again, like I said.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or anything else?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none that I know of.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): How about drink? Alcohol.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, socially. A glass if I'm out, like.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not here to lecture you. A rough amount in a usual week helps me, especially with burning and the liver.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps. I didn't want to say it out straight.

[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Thank you for telling me. That amount can irritate the stomach lining and nudge the liver, so I'll want bloods. I'm not judging the wine, we'll just work with the truth of it.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the liver already damaged? They did bloods before and said the liver was borderline, but I never got a number. Was that last year? I can't remember when.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Borderline without a number doesn't let me say damaged or not. We'll repeat the liver bloods properly, and a full blood count while we're at it.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Will I have to stop the wine altogether? And will that fix the sleep?

[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd like you to cut back, not a cold stop tonight if that panics you. Less in the evening should help both the burning and the waking. We can look at sleep again once the acid is quieter.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): Are you starting me on something? Will it clash with the water tablet?
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Lansoprazole, thirty milligrams, once every morning, half an hour before breakfast, for the acid. It doesn't clash with a water tablet in any way that worries me.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): For how long? Sorry, I keep firing questions. And what if I get side effects? The purple ones gave me a head, I told you.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Try four weeks and then I'll see you. If you feel unwell on it, stop and ring us, but a headache isn't the usual story with this one. Don't take ibuprofen or those anti-inflammatories on top.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I need the camera? My mother had a stomach ulcer and I'm after convincing myself it's the same.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. If it hasn't settled when I see you in four weeks, or if you vomit blood or pass black stools before that, then we arrange a camera test. Come sooner for those, don't wait.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): And the old borderline liver, are you sure repeating it is enough? Should I be in the hospital?

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): For what you've told me today, outpatient bloods are the right next step. My working impression is acid-related pain, gastritis or reflux, with the wine in the mix. I can't fully rule out an ulcer, which is why the safety net and the review matter.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I'll try the tablet and I'll mind the wine. I'll be worrying until the bloods come back, but at least there's a plan.

spec.situation: Person attending for stomach pain and poor sleep; alcohol answered casually ('socially'), later 'a bottle of wine most nights, perhaps'; doctor non-judgemental; liver blood tests ordered; stomach medicine started.
features: vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

bad.reason: Head symptom and not every day supported; 'present/current headache' not stated, only Crocin used 'when it's at me'.

bad.reason: Prior liver bloods said 'borderline' supported, but status 'completed' applies to prior tests without clear doctor confirmation.

Nausea was specifically asked about and the answer was equivocal/uncertain ('Sometimes, not really. I don't know how to answer that one'), rather than clearly present or absent.
The previously used 'purple capsules' for the stomach were stopped because they gave her a headache.
The doctor stated lansoprazole does not clash with the patient's water tablet in any way that worries him.
The doctor advised that sleep can be reviewed again once the acid symptoms are quieter.
The doctor explicitly said there was nothing today that meant urgent admission/rushing her in, and later that outpatient bloods rather than hospital admission were the right next step.
